problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}?$

$$
U={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}
$$
worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2},\,{u}_{3}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$, we need to find a fourth vector $x$ such that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}-{x}_{4}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}+4{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 10 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are three pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. From the third and first equation, we get ${x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{5}{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{5}{x}_{4}$, respectively. Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}+2(-\frac{1}{5}{x}_{4})-{x}_{4}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{7}{5}{x}_{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}{x}_{4} \\ -\frac{7}{5}{x}_{4} \\ -\frac{1}{5}{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{4}=5$, we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$ is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Finally, $\,\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}=-\frac{1}{5}.$
